title: 6379249 Canada Inc. (Mar 2015 TCC) Tax Court Decision
subject: TCC appeal on SR&ED eligibility for 2009-2010 miniature printer work and the role of contemporaneous documents.
summary: 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 77, is a Tax Court of Canada decision on SR&ED investment tax credits claimed for 2009 and 2010 miniature-printer work. It applies to Canadian SR&ED claimants. The Court allowed the appeals, holding that system uncertainty existed and that the ITA does not require filing contemporaneous documents, although producing them is strongly advisable.
metaDescription: Learn about the March 2015 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED ruling for 6379249 Canada Inc. and key takeaways for Canadian R&D claims.

body.text: (1) Executive Summary & Case Background
Case Identification and Procedural Posture

On March 31, 2015, the Honourable Justice Johanne D'Auray of the Tax Court of Canada issued a landmark judgment in 6379249 Canada Inc. v. Her Majesty The Queen, 2015 TCC 77 (Court File No. 2012-3634(IT)G). Heard in Montreal, Quebec, over three days in September 2014 under the Court's General Procedure, the appeal concerned assessments issued by the Minister of National Revenue under the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "ITA") for the appellant's 2009 and 2010 taxation years. The dispute centred on the Minister's complete denial of the Scientific Research and Experimental Development ("SR&ED") Investment Tax Credits ("ITCs") claimed by the appellant, in the amounts of $103,628 for its 2009 taxation year and $49,688 for its 2010 taxation year, in respect of a new SR&ED project on its miniature printer that the appellant opened in 2009. Because the appeal proceeded under the General Procedure rather than the Informal Procedure, Justice D'Auray's legal holdings establish formal jurisprudential precedent for Canadian tax practitioners and claimants across all industries.
The Taxpayer's SR&ED Claim

Beginning in 2006, the appellant, 6379249 Canada Inc., embarked on the design and experimental development of a miniature, self-contained wireless portable printer (the "printer"). The technical work was directed by the appellant's Chief Executive Officer, Mr. Raja Tuli, an internationally recognized authority and leading expert in the physical and electronic miniaturization of high-technology equipment. For the initial phases of the project commencing in 2006, the Canada Revenue Agency ("CRA") accepted that the work qualified as eligible SR&ED and granted the corresponding tax incentives.

At the end of 2008, Mr. Tuli believed that the printer's technological objectives had been met and 200 printers were released onto the market; however, after customer complaints and the appellant's own testing of approximately 50 units showed that more than 20 percent did not meet specifications (the paper sometimes came out curled and the battery often drained after five to ten pages instead of lasting for a full 20-sheet cartridge), the printer was withdrawn from the market, and in 2009 the appellant opened a new SR&ED project to resolve the technological uncertainties that remained within the printer's 1.5" x 1.5" x 10" form factor. The appellant claimed SR&ED ITCs for the 2009 and 2010 taxation years on the basis that technological uncertainties still remained at the printer level, so that resolving the interacting physical and mechanical problems of the miniaturized anti-curl and power systems required a hypothesis-driven systematic investigation to overcome "system uncertainty" at the holistic printer level. At trial, the appellant supported its technical position through the viva voce testimony of Mr. Tuli and the expert testimony of Ms. Deborah Frail of R&D Partners, who had served with the firm since its establishment in 2002.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

The Minister of National Revenue denied the appellant's 2009 and 2010 SR&ED claims in their entirety, advancing a comprehensive three-pronged legal and technical challenge. First, relying on the expert report and testimony of Mr. Ted Wierzbica, a holder of a doctorate in metrology and former Vice-President, Engineering at Escher-Grad who joined the CRA's SR&ED directorate in 2000, served as its National Technology Sector Specialist for information technology and had been consulted on the appellant's 2006 and 2007 claims, the Respondent contended that because the appellant had commercially released the printer in 2008, the system-level technological uncertainty of the miniature printer had already been resolved and no new uncertainties existed in 2009 and 2010. The Crown argued that the activities undertaken during the taxation years in dispute consisted of "routine engineering"—specifically, standard engineering work aimed only at fixing the problems reported by users of the already-released printer, which Mr. Wierzbica characterized as "refinements" or "quality oriented work". By evaluating individual engineering tasks in isolation rather than examining the integrated system, the CRA took the position that each activity (the sourcing of felt material, the clutch surface, the analysis of static versus dynamic friction regimes, the optimisation of the electric motor control algorithm, and the analysis of paper moisture content) was standard engineering drawing on common knowledge and therefore involved no technological uncertainty.

Second, the Respondent challenged the existence of a "systematic investigation or search" on evidentiary grounds, pointing out that the appellant had not filed in evidence any contemporaneous technical documentation, experimental logs, or written test protocols describing its systematic investigation during the 2009 and 2010 taxation years. Third, on procedural grounds and in respect of the 2010 taxation year only, the Respondent asserted that the appellant was statutorily barred from claiming the SR&ED expenditures because it had allegedly failed to file Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) containing the requisite "prescribed information" (namely, the scientific report that the form indicated was attached) within the strict 12-month filing deadline following its corporate income tax return due date (18 months after the end of the taxation year, which for the appellant's taxation year ended March 31, 2010 was September 30, 2011) as mandated by subsection 37(11) of the ITA.
Governing Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework

The legal eligibility of R&D tax incentives in Canada is governed by the interplay of three primary provisions of the ITA and an established body of Tax Court of Canada jurisprudence. At the foundation of the regime lies subsection 248(1) of the ITA, which defines "scientific research and experimental development" as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". For industrial claimants, paragraph (c) of the definition encompasses "experimental development," namely work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Crucially, paragraphs (e) through (k) explicitly exclude specific commercial and routine activities from SR&ED eligibility, most notably paragraph 248(1)(f), which disqualifies "quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes".

Financial deductibility and tax credit calculations are governed by subsections 37(1), 37(11), and 127(9) of the ITA. Subsection 37(1) permits a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct current SR&ED expenditures via a cumulative expenditure pool mechanism. However, this substantive right is strictly conditioned on subsection 37(11), which stipulates that no amount may be deducted under subsection 37(1) in respect of an expenditure unless the taxpayer files with the Minister a prescribed form (Form T661) containing "prescribed information" (on the current Form T661, the technical narratives in Part 2, boxes 242, 244, and 246; in this case, the "scientific report" that the appellant stated accompanied its Form T661) on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year. Parallel time limits under paragraph 127(9)(m) govern the inclusion of "qualified expenditures" in the SR&ED ITCs defined in subsection 127(9), which are deductible under subsection 127(5) and, where the taxpayer qualifies, refundable under section 127.1.

In evaluating whether a project satisfies subsection 248(1), Canadian courts apply the canonical five-question test formulated by Chief Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] T.C.J. No. 340 (QL), 98 DTC 1839, which mandates that SR&ED legislation be given a fair, large, and liberal construction to ensure the attainment of its object of encouraging scientific research in Canada. First, the Court asks whether there was a technical risk or technological uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Second, the Court examines whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the Court assesses whether the procedures adopted accorded with established and objective principles of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Fourth, the Court determines whether the process resulted in a technological advance, meaning an advancement in the general understanding of technology. Fifth, although the ITA itself contains no explicit statutory mandate requiring contemporaneous documentation, the Court considers whether a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results was kept as the work progressed; in the present judgment, however, Justice D'Auray applied these considerations through three condensed criteria at paragraph 59: scientific or technological uncertainty, a systematic investigation by means of experiment or analysis (including the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses), and work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement.

Furthermore, in Northwest Hydraulic, Chief Justice Bowman recognized the CRA's former Information Circular 86-4R3 ("IC 86-4R3") as a useful and reliable guide to interpreting subsection 248(1). In a vital jurisprudential update at paragraphs 57 and 58 of 6379249 Canada Inc., Justice D'Auray formally confirmed that the CRA's December 2012 consolidated policy document—Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (the "2012 CRA SR&ED Policy")—which replaced IC 86-4R3, is likewise a "useful and reliable guide" for the Court, while reiterating that administrative guidelines remain legally subordinate to the statutory text of the ITA.
The Court's Final Holding

Justice D'Auray allowed the appellant's appeals for both the 2009 and 2010 taxation years in full and awarded costs against the Crown. The Court rejected the Respondent's attempt to fragment the project into isolated engineering tasks, holding that the appellant faced genuine system uncertainty at the holistic printer level throughout 2009 and 2010. The Court held that Mr. Wierzbica had put too much emphasis on the 2008 commercial release of the printer and, in doing so, ignored the essential fact that the printer did not function and had to be removed from the market; Mr. Wierzbica himself conceded in cross-examination that, absent the commercial release, the 2009 and 2010 work would most probably have been accepted as SR&ED. Moreover, Justice D'Auray rejected the Respondent's submissions that the felt testing, the slip-clutch redesign, the static versus dynamic friction analysis, the new printer driver and the paper-moisture jig were matters of common knowledge; relying on the French version of paragraph (c), which covers even a slight improvement ("même légère"), she found that each of these activities was undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement, adding that any 2010 work falling outside paragraph (c) would be caught by paragraph (d).

Addressing the critical evidentiary dispute at paragraphs 71, 72, and 92, Justice D'Auray held that while the appellant did not file any contemporaneous documents describing its systematic investigation, the ITA contains no legislative requirement that such documents be filed as a pre-condition of eligibility. While observing that it would have been better if the appellant had produced such records (which Mr. Tuli testified filled boxes) or, if too voluminous, at least a sample of them, the Court found Mr. Tuli to be a credible witness whose detailed oral testimony established that hypotheses were formulated, tested, analyzed, and iteratively modified. Finally, on the subsection 37(11) procedural bar, which concerned only the 2010 taxation year, the Court noted that both parties had introduced little evidence on timeliness and that most of it was hearsay: the T2 return bore a CRA receipt stamp of September 30, 2011 at 4:16 p.m. but the scientific report did not, and the accountant who hand-delivered the package was not called to testify, while Mr. Tuli credibly testified that the appellant would never have filed its return without the scientific report. Describing the question as "not an easy call," the Court gave the appellant the benefit of the doubt and accepted, on a balance of probabilities, that the scientific report had been filed with the Form T661 on September 30, 2011, within the statutory deadline.
(2) Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

Although 6379249 Canada Inc. ultimately prevailed before the Tax Court of Canada, from a tax risk management and legal advisory perspective, the case represents a near-fatal compliance breakdown. Having enjoyed smooth SR&ED claim approvals beginning in 2006, the taxpayer suffered a complete disallowance of its 2009 and 2010 claims at the audit and objection stages, forcing it to endure years of frozen working capital and costly General Procedure tax litigation. An examination of the judgment reveals five core legal, technical, and evidentiary vulnerabilities that triggered the CRA's reassessment and exposed the taxpayer to severe litigation risk.
Complete Absence of Contemporaneous Documentary Evidence of Systematic Investigation

The single greatest operational failure identified in the ruling is recorded at paragraphs 71 and 92 of Justice D'Auray's judgment: the appellant did not file in evidence any contemporaneous documents describing its systematic investigation. In Canadian SR&ED administration, the fifth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic states that a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results should be kept as the work progresses. CRA Research and Technology Advisors ("RTAs") treat contemporaneous documentation—generated during the taxation year as the experimental development unfolds—as the primary verification mechanism for proving that a structured scientific method occurred rather than ad-hoc troubleshooting.

When 6379249 Canada Inc. came to trial without producing structured experimental logs, bench notebooks, quantitative failure matrices, or dated design-iteration records (even though Mr. Tuli testified that he had recorded each hypothesis, test and result and had boxes of such records), the Respondent argued that there was no documentary proof that a systematic investigation had taken place. At trial, Justice D'Auray salvaged the appellant's claim by drawing a sharp legal distinction between an administrative expectation and a statutory requirement: because subsection 248(1) and section 37 of the ITA do not legislate mandatory document retention for the technical process itself, a claimant is legally permitted to prove its systematic investigation via credible oral testimony on a balance of probabilities.

However, Canadian tax practitioners must recognize that the appellant's victory on this point was an extraordinary exception driven by the unique personal profile of its CEO, Mr. Tuli, an internationally renowned miniaturization pioneer whom the Respondent's own expert acknowledged as the leading expert in the field, and who explained in detail on the witness stand each hypothesis, test and result, which he stated he had recorded in boxes of records that were never filed in evidence. Justice D'Auray explicitly observed at paragraph 71 that, although the ITA does not require such documents to be filed, it would have been better if the appellant had produced its records or, if too voluminous, at least a sample of them. Subsequent Tax Court of Canada decisions citing 6379249 Canada Inc.—including Highweb & Page Group Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 137), ACSIS EHR (Electronic Health Record) Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 263), Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6), and Concept Danat Inc. v. The Queen (2019 TCC 32)—have repeatedly emphasized that taxpayers who come to court without proper contemporaneous documentation to substantiate their thought process and experimental steps will almost invariably see their appeals dismissed.
Failure to Frame System Uncertainty Versus Component-Level Routine Engineering

A recurring trigger for CRA disallowances in multi-year engineering projects occurs when a project transitions from early-stage proof-of-concept, where fundamental component feasibility is unknown, to later-stage prototype integration, where components are combined into a constrained production architecture. Because 6379249 Canada Inc. had commercially released the printer in 2008 after claiming SR&ED on it since 2006, the CRA and its expert witness, Mr. Wierzbica, concluded that the system-level uncertainty had been resolved and then viewed the 2009 and 2010 activities through a reductionist lens: they isolated individual activities (felt sourcing, the clutch surface, the static versus dynamic friction analysis, the motor control algorithm and the moisture analysis), concluded that each was standard engineering, and classified the entire effort as "routine engineering". Indeed, the Respondent's position was that, the printer having already been released commercially, the 2009 and 2010 work was aimed only at fixing problems reported by users rather than at achieving technological advancement, although Mr. Wierzbica conceded that, had the printer not been released, the project would most probably have been accepted.

The judgment does not examine the content of the appellant's technical submissions; the dispute was triggered instead by the 2008 commercial release, which the CRA treated as proof that system uncertainty had been resolved, so a claimant in a similar position should rigorously articulate in its technical narratives (Form T661, Part 2, boxes 242, 244, and 246) why system uncertainty persisted. Consistent with the expert evidence accepted by Justice D'Auray in 6379249 Canada Inc. (and later reinforced in Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 42), technological uncertainty does not require that a taxpayer invent a wholly novel law of physics; rather, system uncertainty arises when known components or standard technologies are integrated into an architecture with such severe, competing physical or operational constraints that their combined behaviour cannot be predicted from publicly available engineering knowledge. In the appellant's printer, for example, the choice of felt in the slip clutch affected both the paper tension of the anti-curl system and the power drawn by the motor (the best-quality felt actually caused the motor to stall more often), and the clutch could not simply be enlarged without changing the size of the printer. When a claimant's Form T661 narrative describes what physical components were modified without mathematically and physically defining the inter-systemic conflicts that rendered standard engineering formulas inadequate, the CRA routinely rejects the claim as standard product design.
Vulnerability to Hindsight Bias and Mischaracterization of Observation and Measurement

During the 2009 and 2010 taxation years, the appellant relied heavily on physical observation and measurement to diagnose failure modes in its miniature printer prototypes and refine its design parameters. The CRA disallowed the claim on the premise that the printer's system uncertainty had been resolved upon its commercial release and that the remaining work consisted of standard engineering "refinements" or "quality oriented work"; at trial, the Respondent added that the difference between static and dynamic motor power consumption, motor-control algorithms and the effect of moisture on paper were all common knowledge, and that there was nothing scientific about building a jig.

While Justice D'Auray overturned the CRA's assessment—relying on Chief Justice Bowman's statements in Northwest Hydraulic that technological uncertainty exists in the mind of the specialist who identifies and articulates it, and that routine engineering describes techniques, procedures and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field—the taxpayer's vulnerability stemmed from failing to produce in evidence the records that, according to Mr. Tuli, documented the causal link between hypothesis formulation and observation or measurement. As the Tax Court later demonstrated in Concept Danat Inc. v. The Queen (2019 TCC 32) and Flavor Net Inc., adjusting existing machine settings or testing multiple parameter combinations via trial and error without going beyond normal operating ranges or formulating causal scientific hypotheses does not constitute the scientific method. In 6379249 Canada Inc., the absence from the evidentiary record of written test plans mapping each physical measurement to a specific, falsifiable hypothesis allowed the Respondent to characterize the appellant's systematic experimental work as mere refinements and quality-oriented work.
Procedural Exposure Under Subsection 37(11) for Timely Filing of Prescribed Information

Beyond substantive technical eligibility, the dispute in 6379249 Canada Inc. involved a potentially fatal statutory compliance challenge under subsection 37(11) of the ITA. Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m), a taxpayer is statutorily prohibited from deducting SR&ED expenditures or claiming SR&ED ITCs unless Form T661 containing the "prescribed information" is filed with the Minister within 12 months after the taxpayer's T2 income tax return filing-due date, creating an absolute 18-month deadline from the end of the corporate taxation year. The Tax Court of Canada has consistently affirmed that the technical project descriptions required in boxes 242, 244, and 246 of Form T661 constitute "prescribed information" for the purposes of subsection 37(11), and that the 18-month filing deadline is a strict statutory rule with no ministerial or judicial discretion to grant extensions.

In 6379249 Canada Inc., the CRA objection officer found that the scientific report referred to as attached to the appellant's Form T661 for its 2010 taxation year was missing from the file, prompting the Crown to argue that the 2010 claim was statute-barred under subsection 37(11). Although every page of the appellant's T2 return was stamped by the CRA as received on September 30, 2011 at 4:16 p.m., the scientific report that it said accompanied the return bore no stamp, and the accountant who hand-delivered the sealed envelope on the last filing day was never called to testify, forcing the issue to be decided at trial on largely hearsay evidence and Mr. Tuli's credibility. Fortunately for the appellant, the Court found that most of the evidence of both parties on this point was hearsay (including the Respondent's reliance on two letters from Mr. Tuli's father, who was not called as a witness), that the objection officer's testimony was not determinative, and that Mr. Tuli, who had not delivered the documents himself but testified that the return would never have been filed without the scientific report, was credible; it therefore gave the appellant the benefit of the doubt. Had the Crown presented direct testimony from the intake officers or had Mr. Tuli's recollection been less certain, the 2010 SR&ED claim would have been invalidated on procedural grounds alone, notwithstanding its technical victory under subsection 248(1).
Expenditure Substantiation, Labour Allocation, and Contractual Governance Risks

In Canadian SR&ED litigation, technical documentation deficiencies are inextricably linked to financial expenditure disallowances under subsections 37(1) and 127(9). When a taxpayer fails to maintain or produce contemporaneous project records, as the appellant failed to produce them in 6379249 Canada Inc., it creates an immediate secondary vulnerability (although the amount of the appellant's expenditures was not itself in dispute in that appeal) regarding the substantiation of T4 employee labour hours, materials consumed or transformed, and Canadian contractor payments. As illustrated in parallel Tax Court rulings such as Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 65) and Concept Danat Inc. v. The Queen (2019 TCC 32), even if a project's technical eligibility is debated, the Court requires an accurate, verifiable record of hours worked by specific employees on eligible SR&ED tasks rather than arbitrary management estimates such as applying a flat percentage of payroll. Furthermore, where third-party engineering contractors are engaged, generic consulting invoices that fail to segregate eligible experimental development performed in Canada from routine commercial engineering, or contracts that fail to vest SR&ED intellectual property rights in the claimant, routinely result in expenditure disqualification.
(3) Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement examined in 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 77) against the specific operational or evidentiary deficiency that triggered the CRA's denial and the legal standard of proof articulated by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Tax Court of Canada Standard of Proof & Holding (2015 TCC 77)

cells: 1. Existence of Technological Uncertainty vs. Routine Engineering
ITA s. 248(1) definition of SR&ED; Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 1; 2012 CRA SR&ED Policy s. 2.1.1.

After the printer's 2008 commercial release failed (over 20 percent of units curled paper or drained the battery after five to ten pages) and the printer was withdrawn, the taxpayer opened a new SR&ED project in 2009 without producing in evidence documents explaining why standard engineering could not resolve the remaining system-level problems.

The Crown and its expert (Mr. Wierzbica) argued that the 2008 commercial release showed that the system uncertainty had been resolved, and then evaluated tasks in isolation, arguing that each was standard engineering amounting to "refinements" or "quality oriented work".

Balance of Probabilities (System-Level Analysis): The Court rejected the CRA's isolated-task approach and held that Mr. Wierzbica put too much emphasis on the commercial release, ignoring that the printer did not function and had to be removed from the market (paras. 68–69, 103). A claimant satisfies Criterion 1 by proving system uncertainty at the integrated product/system level where extreme miniaturization creates unpredictable component interactions.
2. Formulation of Specific Hypotheses
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 2; Form T661 Box 242 / 244.

Although Mr. Tuli testified that he recorded each hypothesis, test and result (and had boxes of such records), the taxpayer did not produce any of these records in evidence for the 2009 and 2010 taxation years.

The Respondent argued that the appellant had not filed in evidence any documents demonstrating that it had followed a systematic approach, and that the work performed on each activity was routine engineering.

Credible Viva Voce Reconstruction of Hypothesis Cycles: While written hypotheses are strongly preferred, the Court held that detailed, credible oral testimony from the lead researcher (Mr. Tuli) demonstrating that specific causal hypotheses were formulated before each design iteration satisfies the statutory threshold.
3. Accordance with the Scientific Method (Observation & Measurement)
ITA s. 248(1) & s. 248(1)(f) exclusion; Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 3.

The taxpayer relied heavily on standard physical observation and measurement techniques to evaluate prototype failures without producing in evidence contemporaneous test protocols distinguishing these activities from routine quality control.

The CRA contended that the work consisted of "refinements" or "quality oriented work", and the Respondent argued that friction-regime differences, motor-control algorithms and the effect of moisture on paper were common knowledge and that there was nothing scientific about building a jig.

Intent, Context, and Iterative Analysis: Citing Northwest Hydraulic, the Court described a systematic investigation as operating within the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement and experiment (para. 70). Applying known measurement tools to test hypotheses and iteratively refine an uncertain system is eligible SR&ED; the Court also accepted that building a moisture jig for such a small roll of paper was far from obvious and held that, if the 2010 work did not fall within paragraph (c), it would be caught by paragraph (d).
4. Achievement of Technological Advancement
ITA s. 248(1)(c); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 4; Zeuter Development (2006 TCC 597).

Because the taxpayer's 2009–2010 work followed a failed commercial release, it was exposed to the characterization that it merely fixed problems reported by users rather than generating new technological knowledge relative to the 2006–2008 baseline.

The Respondent argued that the objective of a small printer with many contributing technologies had been achieved by the 2008 commercial release, that the 2009–2010 work only fixed user-reported problems, and that each activity (including the new printer driver, from which no new scientific knowledge was gained) was routine engineering.

Advancement of the Technological Knowledge Base: Relying on the French version of paragraph (c) ("même légère"), the Court held that even a slight improvement qualifies, and found technological advancements in the felt experiment, the identification of static versus dynamic motor load as the main factor in battery life, the concentric-ridge clutch design, the calibrated new printer driver and the moisture-jig work, with paragraph (d) as a fallback for the 2010 work (paras. 97–103).
5. Contemporaneous Documentation of Systematic Investigation
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 5; 6379249 Canada Inc. paras. 71, 72, 92.
The appellant did not file in evidence any contemporaneous documents describing its systematic investigation for the 2009 and 2010 taxation years.

The Respondent asserted that the total absence of contemporaneous experimental documentation was fatal to the appellant's claim, as there was no objective documentary proof of a systematic investigation.

Statutory Distinction vs. Evidentiary Weight: Justice D'Auray ruled at paras. 71–72 and 92 that the ITA contains no legislative requirement to file contemporaneous technical documents. A taxpayer may prove its case via oral testimony of a highly credible witness (Mr. Tuli) corroborated by expert evidence (Ms. Frail), though the Court stated that it would have been better if the appellant had produced its records or at least a sample of them (para. 71).
6. Administrative Policy Interpretive Weight
IC 86-4R3; 2012 CRA SR&ED Policy; 6379249 Canada Inc. paras. 57–58.

The taxpayer's 2009–2010 claims and the December 2010 and November 2011 assessments predated the 2012 CRA SR&ED Policy, issued on December 19, 2012, which the Court nonetheless relied upon where appropriate.

The CRA, through its expert (a former CRA National Technology Sector Specialist), analyzed the work activity by activity rather than at the system/printer level in order to disqualify the 2009–2010 work.

Useful and Reliable Guide Subordinate to Statute: At paras. 57–58, Justice D'Auray confirmed that the 2012 CRA SR&ED Policy (like IC 86-4R3 before it) is a "useful and reliable guide," but remains subordinate to the ITA, which governs in case of conflict; separately, at para. 56, the Court recalled that SR&ED legislation must receive a fair, large and liberal construction because the incentives are intended to encourage scientific research in Canada.
7. Timely Filing of Prescribed Information on Form T661

For its 2010 taxation year, the taxpayer's hand-delivered T2 return was stamped as received on September 30, 2011 (the last filing day), but its scientific report (the "prescribed information") bore no CRA stamp, and the accountant who delivered it did not testify.

The Crown argued that, for the 2010 taxation year, the appellant failed to file the prescribed information (its scientific report) with its Form T661 within the mandatory time limit of subsection 37(11), rendering the expenditures non-deductible by operation of law.

Balance of Probabilities on Filing Evidence: Subsection 37(11) is a strict statutory bar, and under subsection 37(12) an expenditure not reported on time is deemed not to be an SR&ED expenditure; in this case, the "prescribed information" at issue was the appellant's scientific report. However, noting that most of the evidence of both parties was hearsay and that this was "not an easy call," the Court found Mr. Tuli credible, gave the appellant the benefit of the doubt and accepted on a balance of probabilities that the scientific report was filed with the T661 on September 30, 2011 (paras. 119–127).

body.text: (4) Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the jurisprudential lessons of 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 77) into actionable tax and engineering governance, the following two applied industry case studies demonstrate how Canadian corporations facing the exact legal and evidentiary pitfalls identified by Justice D'Auray can restructure their operations to achieve audit-proof compliance under subsections 248(1), 37(1), 37(11), and 127(9) of the ITA.
Case Study 1: Mechatronic Miniaturization and System-Level Uncertainty in Medical Wearable Hardware
Fact Pattern and Identified Legal Pitfalls

MedVitals MicroSystems Inc. ("MedVitals"), a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation ("CCPC") based in Montreal, Quebec, is in Year 4 of developing a self-contained, coin-sized wireless continuous hemodynamic monitoring patch. During Years 1 and 2, MedVitals claimed and received refundable 35% federal SR&ED ITCs (and Quebec R&D tax credits) for developing its proprietary optical bio-sensor. In Year 4, MedVitals incurs $1.4 million in T4 engineering wages, prototype materials, and Canadian contract engineering fees to miniaturize the entire device enclosure by 60% while integrating a micro-battery, Bluetooth Low Energy ("BLE") antenna, microfluidic sweat channel, and optical sensor onto a single flexible substrate. Every individual sub-component utilizes commercially known fabrication techniques. The engineering team conducts hundreds of benchtop thermal, RF-attenuation, and mechanical flexure measurements, modifying the layout after each failure, but records only final CAD revisions in its product lifecycle management ("PLM") software without written hypotheses or test logs. Furthermore, MedVitals relies on an external accountant to mail a paper addendum containing its Form T661 Part 2 technical narratives near the 18-month statutory filing deadline without certified tracking.

This fact pattern mirrors the exact vulnerabilities of 6379249 Canada Inc.: a high risk of CRA disallowance on the grounds that Year 4 integration of known components is "routine engineering"; vulnerability to a CRA allegation that standard benchtop observation and measurement constitute routine testing under paragraph 248(1)(f); a failure to produce contemporaneous documentation proving a systematic investigation, the gap noted at paragraphs 71 and 92 of 2015 TCC 77; and catastrophic procedural exposure under subsection 37(11) regarding timely filing of prescribed information.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance to Isolate System Uncertainty

To defeat a CRA "routine engineering" challenge based on the use of known sub-components, MedVitals must restructure its internal SR&ED project governance to mirror Justice D'Auray's holding on system uncertainty at paragraphs 69 and 103 and throughout 6379249 Canada Inc.. Rather than defining the SR&ED project around commercial product features or isolated component adjustments, the Vice-President of Engineering must establish a formal SR&ED Project Charter that defines the System-Level Technological Baseline. This baseline must document why publicly available engineering principles, vendor datasheets, and standard electronic design automation ("EDA") or CAD simulation models cannot predict the coupled multiphysics interactions when the optical emitter, BLE RF transceiver, and microfluidic channel are compressed within a sub-3-millimetre separation boundary.

Simultaneously, to prevent the CRA from arguing that the core technological uncertainty was already resolved during Years 1 and 2 (analogous to the 2006–2008 versus 2009–2010 dispute in 6379249 Canada Inc.), the governance charter must formally close the initial "Sensor Feasibility" phase and open a distinct SR&ED project titled Resolution of Coupled Electro-Thermal and RF-Dielectric System Uncertainties in Sub-Millimetre Flexible Substrates. Specifically, the charter must quantify the competing physical constraints across sub-systems—for example, demonstrating that increasing optical LED drive current to compensate for epidermal scattering induces localized Joule heating (P = I²R), which simultaneously warps the flexible polyimide substrate beyond focal tolerances and detunes the adjacent BLE impedance matching network.
Step 2: Restructuring Technical Documentation and Form T661 Narratives (Boxes 242, 244, 246)

To eliminate the evidentiary gamble reflected in Justice D'Auray's comments at paragraphs 71, 72, and 92—where the taxpayer, having filed none of its records in evidence, relied solely on oral testimony at trial—MedVitals must embed mandatory contemporaneous documentation into its bi-weekly engineering sprints and map those records directly to the "prescribed information" fields of Form T661. In Box 242 (Scientific or Technological Uncertainties), the technical narrative must explicitly distinguish routine technical problems from system-level technological uncertainty in accordance with section 2.1.1 of the 2012 CRA SR&ED Policy endorsed at paragraphs 57 and 58 of 2015 TCC 77. The narrative should articulate that while standard RF antenna tuning and flexible PCB routing are known engineering practices in isolation, a system-level technological uncertainty arose because standard electromagnetic and thermo-mechanical models failed to predict parasitic capacitive coupling and substrate delamination when the optical driver and BLE antenna shared a 150-micron elastomeric dielectric layer under cyclic biomechanical strain.

For Box 244 (Work Performed in the Taxation Year), MedVitals must implement a mandatory digital SR&ED Experimentation Matrix inside its Jira and PLM workflow so that every CAD revision or prototype build is gated by a contemporaneous record generated before and immediately after testing. Each record must state the exact causal hypothesis being tested prior to fabrication—such as testing whether introducing a 40-micron perforated copper ground-plane lattice between the optical driver and BLE trace will attenuate near-field parasitic coupling by at least 12 dB while maintaining substrate flexural modulus below 3 GPa. The record must then link standard measurement tools (vector network analyzers, infrared thermography, and optical profilometry) directly to the validation of that hypothesis so the CRA cannot dismiss those activities as routine quality control under paragraph 248(1)(f). Finally, the log must record raw measured datasets against predicted theoretical values and document how the rejection of a failed hypothesis constitutes a valid step in the scientific method under Northwest Hydraulic Criteria 3 and 4, leading to the iterative modification of the next hypothesis. In Box 246 (Technological Advancements Achieved), MedVitals must frame the advancement not as the commercial creation of the miniature patch—which Zeuter Development confirms is insufficient on its own—but as the generation of new, proprietary engineering knowledge quantifying the dielectric-thermal-mechanical boundary laws governing ultra-dense flexible mechatronic packaging.
Step 3: Restructuring Contractual Terms for Canadian Subcontractors

To protect the eligibility of its contract engineering expenditures under subsections 37(1) and 127(9) of the ITA, MedVitals must replace generic "product design and fabrication consulting" master service agreements with itemized SR&ED Statements of Work ("SOWs"). Each SOW must specify that the arm's-length contractor is a Canadian resident performing the experimental work physically within Canada on MedVitals' behalf. The contract must explicitly reference the Hypothesis IDs from MedVitals' SR&ED Experimentation Matrix, stipulate that the contractor must deliver raw experimental test logs and simulation failure data as a condition of milestone payment, and include an unambiguous intellectual property clause vesting 100% ownership and exploitation rights of all resulting SR&ED data, discoveries, and prototypes in MedVitals. Furthermore, MedVitals must require contractors to issue separate invoices (or distinct line-item billing codes) separating eligible experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c) from ineligible commercial tooling, regulatory compliance certification, or routine production quality control under paragraph 248(1)(f).
Step 4: Financial Substantiation and Subsection 37(11) Filing Controls

To prevent both expenditure reductions (as seen in Hypercube and Concept Danat) and the subsection 37(11) procedural bar contested in 6379249 Canada Inc., MedVitals must overhaul its financial and tax filing controls. Where MedVitals elects the Prescribed Proxy Amount ("PPA") method under subsection 127(9) to calculate overhead at 55% of directly engaged T4 salaries, it must replace year-end percentage estimates with weekly electronic timesheets requiring all T4 engineers to log hours directly against specific SR&ED Hypothesis IDs, strictly excluding bonuses, shareholder dividends, and commercial administrative time. In addition, an inventory tracking code in the ERP system must log every flexible PCB wafer, micro-battery, and optical sensor destroyed during destructive prototype testing ("materials consumed") or permanently integrated into non-commercial experimental prototypes ("materials transformed"), deducting any scrap or salvage value.

Finally, to eliminate the paper-filing hearsay dispute encountered in 6379249 Canada Inc., MedVitals must mandate that its complete T2 corporate income tax return, Schedule T2SCH31, and Form T661 (with Boxes 242, 244, and 246 fully populated) be transmitted electronically via CRA Corporation Internet Filing at least 60 days prior to the 12-month post-filing due date (18 months after fiscal year-end). MedVitals must retain the automated CRA electronic confirmation number, a cryptographic hash of the transmitted T2-T661 submission package, and an archived copy of the CRA My Business Account timestamped receipt in its permanent corporate tax audit file.
Case Study 2: Distributed Embedded Firmware and High-Speed Industrial Optical Sorting
Fact Pattern and Identified Legal Pitfalls

AgriSort Photonics Ltd. ("AgriSort"), an Ontario-based industrial automation manufacturer, designs high-speed optical sorting machinery for agricultural processing. In its 2025 taxation year, AgriSort attempts to integrate an off-the-shelf hyperspectral short-wave infrared ("SWIR") camera, a real-time FPGA image-processing board, and a high-pressure pneumatic ejector manifold to detect and eject mycotoxin-contaminated grain kernels moving on a conveyor at 4.5 metres per second. When AgriSort initially tests the integrated system using the camera and pneumatic valve manufacturers' standard settings, the system fails to accurately eject contaminated kernels due to motion blur, variable kernel geometry, and aerodynamic turbulence in the ejection zone. Over an eight-month period, AgriSort's lead engineer and five technicians test thousands of combinations of camera exposure times, conveyor speeds, illumination angles, and air-jet pulse durations. Eventually, they also rewrite the FPGA embedded firmware to implement a custom predictive trajectory algorithm and modify the physical nozzle manifold geometry. However, in filing its SR&ED claim, AgriSort describes the project broadly as "testing 10,000 parameter combinations of camera and air-valve settings to optimize sorting accuracy," fails to keep written records of its algorithm iterations, and estimates its labour claim by applying a flat 25% allocation across all shop-floor and engineering staff.

This scenario directly implicates the core legal boundary separating 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 77), where the taxpayer won, from Concept Danat Inc. v. The Queen (2019 TCC 32), which cited 6379249 Canada Inc. at paragraphs 57 and 58 but dismissed the taxpayer's appeal. In Concept Danat, the taxpayer adjusted existing laser and printing machine settings (air, power, speed, and temperature) across 10,000 combinations within the equipment's normal operating ranges without modifying the underlying machine architecture, and relied on a flat 10.2% management payroll estimate. The Tax Court dismissed the appeal, holding that operating within existing equipment setting ranges via trial and error does not involve technological uncertainty or the scientific method, and that flat payroll estimates are unacceptable under Hypercube Inc.. Conversely, in 6379249 Canada Inc., the taxpayer went beyond known operating parameters to engineer novel system-level hardware and firmware interactions through hypothesis-driven testing. Because AgriSort has conflated its ineligible parameter-tuning phase with its genuinely eligible embedded firmware and aerodynamic manifold redesign—and lacked contemporaneous labour and experimental records—its entire claim faces imminent disallowance by the CRA.
Step 1: Project Governance — Bifurcating Routine Parameter Tuning from System-Level Experimental Development

To survive judicial scrutiny under the 6379249 Canada Inc. and Concept Danat standard, AgriSort's tax advisor and Engineering Director must immediately bifurcate the project timeline and scope into two legally distinct phases. All time and materials expended adjusting the off-the-shelf SWIR camera exposure settings, conveyor speeds, and pneumatic valve durations within the manufacturers' specified operating ranges must be carved out and classified as ineligible routine engineering and standard equipment calibration. However, the documented failure of this initial calibration phase serves a vital legal function: it establishes the empirical proof that the current state of technology and standard operating parameters were insufficient to resolve the problem, thereby marking the exact chronological birth of the technological uncertainty as required by section 2.1.1 of the 2012 CRA SR&ED Policy cited in 2015 TCC 77 at paragraphs 57 and 58.

AgriSort must establish the formal start of the SR&ED project at the exact milestone where the engineering team abandoned standard parameter combinations and initiated structural modifications to the underlying technology. Specifically, the SR&ED project scope must be restricted to re-architecting the FPGA hardware-description language ("HDL") pipeline to process 240-band hyperspectral cubes in under 1.2 milliseconds without frame-buffer overflow, and redesigning the internal fluid dynamics of the pneumatic manifold to eliminate boundary-layer turbulence at 800 Hz actuation frequencies.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Quantitative Experimentation Tracking

To prevent the CRA from dismissing the firmware and fluid-dynamic iterations as unrecorded trial and error—and to avoid the evidentiary peril of paragraph 71 of 6379249 Canada Inc.—AgriSort must implement a structured technical documentation protocol across both software and hardware streams. For the embedded FPGA firmware development, AgriSort must configure its Git version-control repository so that every experimental branch commit message is structured around the Northwest Hydraulic scientific method. Each commit header must document the exact memory-bandwidth and deterministic latency bottleneck in the FPGA fabric that prevents standard spectral-angle-mapper algorithms from executing within the 1.2-millisecond flight window of a falling grain kernel, followed by the specific mathematical hypothesis being tested (for example, hypothesizing that replacing 32-bit floating-point covariance matrix inversion with a quantized 8-bit fixed-point bit-shift approximation across 12 orthogonal spectral bands will reduce look-up-table utilization by at least 45% and deterministic latency to under 0.85 milliseconds while maintaining classification false-negative rates below 1.5% under non-uniform illumination).

Simultaneously, AgriSort must configure its optical sorting test rig to export timestamped CSV logs capturing FPGA clock-cycle latency, thermal dissipation, and high-speed stroboscopic shadowgraph measurements of kernel deflection trajectories for each experimental run. As established in 6379249 Canada Inc., these high-speed optical observations and timing measurements are fully eligible SR&ED activities because they are executed systematically to validate or refute a specific causal hypothesis. For the pneumatic manifold redesign, AgriSort must maintain a physical and photographic Prototype Iteration Log in which failed 3D-printed and CNC-machined nozzle prototypes are retained and tagged with a unique Prototype ID corresponding to their computational fluid dynamics ("CFD") hypothesis, acoustic shockwave measurement log, and boundary-layer separation analysis.
Step 3: Contractual Structuring for University and Arm's-Length Engineering Partners

Where AgriSort engages an arm's-length Canadian fluid-dynamics consultancy and a local Canadian university research laboratory to assist with wind-tunnel schlieren imaging, it must structure the contracts to comply with section 37 and subsection 127(9) of the ITA. The agreement with the arm's-length engineering firm must be structured as a contract for SR&ED performed on the taxpayer's behalf (eligible at 80% for ITC calculation purposes), ensuring that the contract explicitly describes the experimental CFD modelling and shockwave testing tied to AgriSort's manifold hypotheses, confirms that all work is performed in Canada by Canadian residents, and assigns all resulting intellectual property to AgriSort. Conversely, for payments made to the approved Canadian university research institute, AgriSort must document the arrangement as a Third-Party Payment under paragraph 37(1)(a)(ii), ensuring that the contract grants AgriSort the legal right to exploit the results of the university's research in its Canadian business operations and that the requisite project details are properly reported in Part 3 of Form T661.
Step 4: Financial Substantiation, Labour Allocation, and Audit-Readiness Controls

To cure the fatal payroll-estimation flaw highlighted in Hypercube Inc. (2015 TCC 65) and Concept Danat Inc. (2019 TCC 32) and satisfy the strict procedural rules of subsection 37(11) addressed in 6379249 Canada Inc., AgriSort must immediately abolish its 25% flat management payroll estimate. The company must implement a daily ERP job-costing timecard system where the lead engineer and technicians log exact hours against specific SR&ED work-orders (such as WO-SRD-102: FPGA Fixed-Point Quantization Hypothesis Testing), strictly separated from commercial work-orders (such as WO-COM-001: Commercial Machine Assembly and Parameter Calibration). Shop-floor technicians' hours must be claimed solely for the exact time spent fabricating experimental manifold prototypes, operating the stroboscopic test rig during hypothesis testing, or executing direct support activities, excluding all hours spent calibrating commercial machines or conducting routine parameter sweeps.

Furthermore, if the modified optical sorter is tested on an active agricultural processing line, AgriSort must strictly apply the CRA's rules distinguishing experimental production from commercial production in conjunction with experimental development. AgriSort may claim only the incremental labour, materials consumed or transformed (such as test batches of grain artificially spiked with fluorescent tracers that must be destroyed after sorting), and direct engineering supervision attributable to resolving the system-level uncertainty, excluding any runs that yield saleable commercial output. Finally, prior to electronic submission of the T2 return and Form T661 within the 18-month statutory window under subsection 37(11), AgriSort must conduct a formal internal mock-audit review to verify that Boxes 242, 244, and 246 contain complete, self-contained technical narratives ("prescribed information") that explicitly cite the contemporaneous Git commit IDs, CFD simulation reports, and test-rig CSV logs. By coupling this contemporaneous evidentiary binder with verifiable electronic filing receipts, AgriSort can substantiate its claim during an initial CRA technical review without ever having to rely on the high-risk courtroom oral testimony defence of 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen.
Summary of Remedial Governance Controls Across Both Case Studies

The following table synthesizes the remedial governance mechanisms designed to inoculate Canadian SR&ED claimants against the specific litigation hazards identified in 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 77) and its subsequent judicial progeny.

cells: Project Framing & Uncertainty Scope
Describing late-stage integration of known components or machine parameter sweeps as eligible R&D.
Establish an SR&ED Project Charter isolating system uncertainty caused by competing multiphysics or latency constraints; carve out pre-SR&ED parameter tuning within normal operating ranges.
